text:
Every table in this course, every key, every join... none of it was obvious once. It all started with one paper, in nineteen seventy. So what came before it?

In the sixties, data lived in trees. IBM's IMS, built to track parts for the Saturn Five rocket, filed each record under its parent. Want Ada's orders? A program starts at the top and follows pointers down. Network databases made the tree a web, but the rule held. The program had to know the ROUTE. So reorganize the file... and every program that walked it breaks.

Then, in June nineteen seventy, Ted Codd, a British-born mathematician at IBM, published an idea that sounds almost too plain. Keep the data in tables, and link rows by value, not by pointer. Order one-oh-one is Ada's because it holds her number, one. So the database can store rows any way it likes. Shuffle them on disk, ask again... the SAME two orders. Codd called that data independence. A program says what it wants... not where to walk.

IBM wasn't sold. IMS made it a fortune, and critics doubted matching values could ever be fast. So its San Jose lab built System R, to find out. It could. Along the way, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce wrote a query language that reads almost like English. They called it Sequel. Trouble was, an aircraft company already owned that name. So out went the vowels... S-Q-L. Boyce died in nineteen seventy-four, still in his twenties. His name lives on in Boyce-Codd normal form.

Here's the twist. IBM published that work, and a small California company read it closely. In seventy-nine, its Oracle was the first SQL database you could buy. IBM's own arrived in eighty-one... the year Codd won the Turing Award. But IBM wasn't the only one reading Codd.
